query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that decouples lattice and electronic heat transport—by independently simulating phonon‐mediated heat conduction using an on‐the‐fly machine‐learned force-field Green–Kubo method and calculating the electronic conductivity via DFT-based Boltzmann transport—will yield significantly more accurate predictions of total thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr than earlier analytical models that conflate the two channels.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory single-phase HfNbTaTiZr alloy produced under controlled conditions; one set of samples is nearly oxygen-free (to represent the ideal, defect‐free state) while the control high-temperature benchmark is an already-characterized specimen containing ~1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.intervention: Implement a fully decoupled simulation pipeline that (a) uses a machine-learning–trained interatomic potential to capture atomic-scale mass and force-constant disorder effects for phonon transport via Green–Kubo molecular dynamics, and (b) computes the electronic transport properties separately using DFT-based Boltzmann transport calculations.
generation.conditions: Evaluations performed over the temperature range of below 200 K (where experiments show comparable lattice and electronic contributions) and from 300 to 1200 K (benchmarking total conductivity for oxygen-containing samples). The oxygen content is controlled to be near-zero for the decoupled lattice and electronic analyses, with comparisons made against a known sample with ~1 wt.% oxygen at high temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The approach mediates predictions by explicitly capturing force-constant fluctuations and chemical disorder at the atomic scale, thereby separately accounting for phonon scattering and electronic band structure effects without imposing a typical Debye-temperature approximation.
generation.mechanism: By isolating phonon dynamics (via ML force-fields in MD simulations) from electron dynamics (via first-principles DFT calculations), the method overcomes the limitations of previous analytical approximations that conflated lattice and electronic conduction. This decoupling is expected to reduce the error in predicted thermal conductivity by a factor of roughly two compared to earlier models that used a single Debye temperature to estimate both contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The primary measured property—total thermal conductivity—will be predicted with separate, quantitatively accurate lattice and electronic contributions. Specifically, for oxygen-free samples below 200 K, the model should show that the phonon and electron channels contribute comparably, and for oxygen-containing samples between 300 and 1200 K, the summed prediction will lie within ±15% of the experimentally observed range (10–17 W/(K·m)).
generation.baseline: Earlier analytical and computational approaches that assume perfect, defect-free single crystals, often relying on a single Debye temperature to parameterize both lattice and electronic transport.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HfNbTaTiZr alloys in well-characterized states: (a) low-temperature (<200 K) measurements to test the decoupled contributions and (b) high-temperature (300–1200 K) cases in samples with 1 wt.% oxygen contamination. Deviations outside these conditions (e.g., substantially different oxygen levels or phase inhomogeneities) are outside the scope of this prediction.
generation.uncertainty: While the decoupling is expected to improve predictive accuracy by roughly a factor of two (error reduced from >50% to about ±15%), the exact quantitative improvement may vary with the precise parameters of the ML force-field training and DFT settings. The contribution of minor defect states not captured by the simulation is also an uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr samples: one with minimal oxygen contamination and one with ~1 wt.% oxygen. For the oxygen-free samples, perform low-temperature (T < 200 K) thermal conductivity measurements that separate lattice and electronic components (e.g., via magneto-thermal measurements or applying a magnetic field to suppress the electronic contribution). For the oxygen-containing samples, measure the total thermal conductivity from 300 to 1200 K. Compare these experimental data with the predictions from the decoupled simulation approach.
measurements: Low-temperature (below 200 K) separate measurements of phonon (lattice) and electronic thermal conductivity.
High-temperature (300–1200 K) total thermal conductivity measurements in oxygen-containing specimens.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the decoupled predictive approach does not yield separate lattice and electronic contributions that, when combined, predict total thermal conductivity within ±15% of the measured values across the specified temperature ranges, or if the predicted temperature dependence fails to match the experimental trend (e.g., comparable contributions below 200 K and the 10–17 W/(K·m) range at high temperature), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy was produced by various methods of powder metallurgy including mechanical alloying, sintering, hot isostatic pressing, spark plasma sintering, and high pressure torsion. The microstructure and mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr prepared by various methods were examined. It was found that the main problem in fabrication of HfNbTaTiZr alloy by powder metallurgy is oxygen contamination. Samples prepared by cold isostatic pressing followed by sintering and/or hot isostatic pressing contained oxygen in the concentration range of 0.55 wt %–0.85 wt %. Oxygen contamination of samples prepared by mechanical alloying was even higher, and the oxygen concentration in these samples exceeded 1 wt %. Oxygen incorporated into the HfNbTaTiZr samples caused deterioration of mechanical properties (embrittlement) and prevented formation of a single phase random solid solution. Investigations performed in the present work showed that the most promising powder metallurgy method of production of HfNbTaTiZr alloy was spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powder. As mentioned in the introduction, it is worth comparing the vibrational dynamics of our HEA to glasses and to crystalline materials with very large unit cells (CMAs), to identify similarities and differences and establish the place of HEAs with respect to these classes of materials. Specifically, as previously said, the low and weakly temperature dependent thermal conductivity in glasses has been associated to the existence of a strong phonon scattering due to the intrinsic disorder. Such regime, characterized by ΓFWHM ∝ (ℏω)4, has been reported in some glasses at energies corresponding to the deviation of the GVDOS from the Debye behavior and has lately been ascribed mostly to the force-constant disorder at a nanometric lengthscale. Interestingly, the same phenomenology arises in random matrix approaches, which model the vibrational properties of a glass through a random network of force-constants over a regular lattice, quite similarly to the case of our HEA,. It is thus important to check weather the same behavior can be found in our HEA, where force-constant fluctuations are the dominant phonon scattering source.
